n: Israel set out with everything he had. At Beer-sheba, the southern border where Abraham and Isaac had worshipped, he offered sacrifices before leaving the promised land.
God spoke to Jacob in a night vision, calling his name twice. Jacob answered with readiness, “Here am I.”

f.g: Repeating a name marks a solemn divine call.

n: God tells Jacob not to fear going to Egypt; there his family will grow into a great nation. Leaving the land was part of God’s plan, as He had foretold to Abraham.

f.w: I will there make of thee a great nation

n: God promises to go with Jacob and bring his family back. Joseph would be at his side when he died, closing his eyes.

f.w: I will go down with thee
Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes
f.g: Joseph will be with you at your death

n: Encouraged, Jacob set out. His sons carried him and their families in Pharaoh’s wagons.
They brought their livestock and possessions and arrived in Egypt—the whole family together.
Every child and grandchild came. This is the moment the twelve-tribe family moves to Egypt, where it will grow into a people.
A list of the family members who came to Egypt begins. Such lists show this was a real family whose descendants became Israel’s tribes.
Reuben’s four sons became the clans of the tribe of Reuben.
Simeon’s sons are listed. One had a Canaanite mother, showing the family did marry outside the covenant line.
Levi’s three sons became the three major divisions of the Levites who would serve at the tabernacle. Moses and Aaron descend from Kohath.
Judah’s sons are listed, recalling chapter 38. Through Pharez and Hezron comes the line of David and, ultimately, Jesus Christ.
Issachar’s four sons are named.
Zebulun’s three sons are named. These are all sons of Leah’s family line.
Leah’s family, including Dinah, totaled thirty-three people. The count likely includes Jacob himself.

f.g: the region of northern Mesopotamia where Jacob lived with Laban

n: Gad’s seven sons are listed. Gad was the son of Leah’s maid Zilpah.
Asher’s family is named, including a daughter, Serah—one of the few women named in these lists.
Zilpah’s descendants numbered sixteen.
Rachel, called here “Jacob’s wife,” had two sons, Joseph and Benjamin.
Joseph’s sons Manasseh and Ephraim were born in Egypt, and are counted in the family, though they did not travel with Jacob.
Benjamin had ten sons listed here—some may be grandsons, as later lists vary.
Rachel’s descendants totaled fourteen.
Dan had one son, Hushim (called Shuham in Numbers). Yet Dan grew into a large tribe.
Naphtali’s four sons are named.
Bilhah, Rachel’s maid, had seven descendants on this list.
Not counting the wives of Jacob’s sons, sixty-six direct descendants traveled to Egypt.
Adding Jacob, Joseph, and Joseph’s two sons gives seventy. Seventy is a number of fullness—the whole family of Israel. Stephen, following the Greek text, gives seventy-five.
Jacob sent Judah ahead to get directions to Goshen. Judah’s leadership role continues to grow.

f.w: to direct his face unto Goshen
f.g: to arrange the way to Goshen

n: Joseph rode out in his chariot to meet his father. They embraced and Joseph wept on his father’s neck for a long time.
Jacob says he can now die in peace, having seen his son alive—a feeling later echoed by Simeon when he held the infant Jesus.
Joseph plans to inform Pharaoh officially that his family has arrived.
Joseph will describe them honestly as shepherds and herdsmen.
Joseph prepares his brothers for the question Pharaoh will ask about their work.
Joseph coaches them to say plainly they are herdsmen. Because Egyptians looked down on shepherds, the family would be settled apart in Goshen—keeping them separate and preserving their identity.
